differences.title: 1. STORAGE MODEL
differences.leftDesc: JanusGraph stores vertices/edges and indices through a configurable persistence layer (e.g., Apache Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB) via storage adapters, enabling horizontal scaling and tailored consistency per backend.
differences.rightDesc: OrientDB can run in embedded, server, or cluster modes, managing graph, document, and other data in its own engine and storage layout. It provides indexing and locking inside the database process.

differences.title: 2. INDEX & SEARCH
differences.leftDesc: JanusGraph uses mixed indexing: local key-based indices plus optional external indexing like Elasticsearch (via JanusGraph integrations) to accelerate predicate queries, while preserving graph traversal semantics.
differences.rightDesc: OrientDB offers native index classes (hash, unique, not unique, full-text where applicable) integrated with its record model. Query plans can exploit indexes directly for both graph and document queries.

differences.title: 3. TRANSACTION & LOCKING
differences.leftDesc: JanusGraph leverages TinkerPop stack concepts: transactions are coordinated with backend-specific locking/atomicity. It often relies on batching writes and careful management of consistency to reduce contention.
differences.rightDesc: OrientDB provides transactional semantics at the record level, coordinating updates within its engine. Depending on mode, it uses internal locking and write-ahead logging to ensure atomicity for graph mutations.

differences.title: 4. QUERY LANGUAGE
differences.leftDesc: JanusGraph is designed around Apache TinkerPop Gremlin traversals, mapping Gremlin steps onto graph operations. This tight integration makes complex traversal pipelines efficient and consistent across backends.
differences.rightDesc: OrientDB supports its SQL dialect for records plus Gremlin for graph traversals. It can execute SQL-based queries and graph traversals in the same system, sharing indexes and execution runtime.

differences.title: 5. GRAPH SCHEMA FLEXIBILITY
differences.leftDesc: JanusGraph typically uses a schema-less feel via property keys and optional edge/vertex labels, with enforcement largely provided by configuration and mapping. It’s optimized for sparse, evolving graphs at scale.
differences.rightDesc: OrientDB supports classes (schema) and schemaless record types. You can define properties and constraints, while still allowing flexible documents; this impacts indexing choices and query validation.

differences.title: 6. VERTEX/EDGE STORAGE & PERFORMANCE
differences.leftDesc: JanusGraph models adjacency via edge-centric storage patterns, with traversal performance heavily influenced by backend data distribution, partitioning keys, and index availability for step predicates.
differences.rightDesc: OrientDB stores records with internal pointers/links and manages traversal-friendly access patterns within its database engine. Performance depends on its indexing, page cache behavior, and link resolution strategies.

differences.title: 7. KNOWLEDGE GRAPH WORKFLOWS
differences.leftDesc: JanusGraph is often used for large-scale knowledge graphs where traversal workloads and distributed storage must scale together. Its adapter model lets you standardize graph operations while swapping infrastructure.
differences.rightDesc: OrientDB fits knowledge-graph workflows that mix graph traversal with document-like payloads in one queryable system. You can co-locate narrative metadata with edges/vertices for richer single-database modeling.
